newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel said to ask Syria, Iran to prevent attack.
newsitem.headline: Israel said to ask Syria, Iran to prevent attack.

text.p: Israel, on high alert against attacks by Islamic Jihad marking the first anniversary of the assassination of the group's leader, has reportedly told Syria and Iran to prevent any such attack.

"We know that both Iran and Syria are centres of operation of terrorist organisations and there is no doubt that they have weight regarding implementation of attacks," Yigal Pressler, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's adviser on "terrorism", told Israel's army radio on Monday.
Local media said Netanyahu sent messages to Syria and Iran demanding they prevent Islamic Jihad from attacking Israel. His spokesman Shai Bazak refused to comment.

On Sunday, security sources said there was information a guerrilla squad was in Israel to avenge the October 26, 1995, assassination in Malta of Islamic Jihad leader Fathi Shqaqi. His killers were not captured. Palestinians blamed Israel.

Israeli newspapers and radio stations said Netanyahu had sent messages via third parties to Syria and Iran. The Jerusalem Post daily said the messages sent over the weekend were relayed to Syria via the United States and to Iran via Germany.
Israeli Public Security Minister Avigdor Kahalani said the expected target was in one of Israel's three largest cities -- Jerusalem, Tel Aviv or Haifa.

Security sources said the high security alert in force since Sunday remained but that measures had been eased somewhat. Roadblocks thrown up by security forces on Sunday snarled traffic throughout the Jewish state.
"The measures were eased but the alert is still on," one security source said.
Witnesses in Jerusalem said security forces were on the streets in large numbers. Usually packed Jerusalem morning rush hour buses had seats available.
The U.S. embassy in Tel Aviv said on Monday that it on Friday issued a notice to American citizens in Israel warning "of increased likelihood of terrorist attacks".
Asked if something had changed to spur an easing of the measures put in place on Sunday, Pressler said:
"Not a lot changed from yesterday to today...The only thing that has changed is the issue of the passage of vehicles toward the large cities which police are directing more efficiently."
He said the alert would continue "until we think there is no intention by terrorist organisations to commit an attack".
Israel's Industrialists Association said on Sunday that the security measures were hurting the economy.

"The increasing jitters are causing serious and significant economic damage. A morning like today causes a situation in which people don't want to go out shopping," said Yehoshua Abramovitch, a spokesman for the association.

Haim Ramon, a leader of Israel's main opposition Labour party, accused Netanyahu's right-wing government of "causing general paralysis and putting the entire population into unnecessary hysterics and panic".
Netanyahu told reporters on Sunday guerrillas were trying to torpedo Israel's peace talks with the Palestinians and said "external elements" were behind the planned attack.

Islamic Jihad and Hamas leaders have been in jail in Palestinian self-rule areas since suicide bombings in February and March, responsibility for which was claimed by Hamas, the other leading Islamic resistance group in Palestinian areas. Those attacks killed 59 people.
